newsitem.title: UK: Emerging markets focus on Yeltsin, US rates.
newsitem.headline: Emerging markets focus on Yeltsin, US rates.

text.p: Emerging market players will be focussing on Russia after last week's announcement that the president will undergo heart surgery, although the U.S. interest rate story will underpin much of this week's activity.

"Apart from the US, the focus is on RUSSIA because prices have come off -- people are trying to assess whether the fall is unreasonable and therefore a buying opportunity, or whether it is a sign of things to come," said Eric Beinstein, emerging market strategist at JP Morgan in London.
"There may not be much more news but people will be assessing the situation."

One Russian debt specialist at a rival firm said investors will be watching the rouble and Russian MinFin bonds, which he said were only moderately affected by the surprise announcement that Russian President Boris Yeltsin would undergo a heart by-pass operation by the end of September.
"They haven't sufficiently priced it in," he said.

While brokers wait to see whether fund managers will step back into the Russian markets next week, U.S. Treasuries will set the market tone as fund managers digest the impact of Friday's non-farm payroll data.

The stronger-than-expected August figure stoked expectations of an early rise in U.S. interest rates -- impacting on emerging debt and equity markets worldwide. Investors are wondering not whether the U.S. will raise rates, but by how much.

"Most markets have factored in a 25 or even a 50 basis point rise -- anything higher would be a bit of a shock," said Suzanne Carrington, who manages Latin America-dedicated funds worth some $200 to $250 million at Flemings Investment Trust.
MEXICO, and ARGENTINA because of the peso's peg to the dollar, remain the most vulnerable to US interest rates rises.

"A 50 b.p. rate rise would be another excuse for the nervous to take money out of Argentina," Carrington said, but added that the impact would be muted because so much money has already left the country since economy minister Domingo Cavallo quit.

Higher U.S. rates will make some investors in Mexico question whether they want to be there at all, especially since the country can ill-afford the likely impact on its currency and its outlook for growth, fund managers say.
In Asia, THAILAND is top of investors' worry list.
"Everything that could go wrong there has gone wrong," said James Hancocks, emerging market fund manager at Guinness Flight.

The country's current account deficit has been revised higher, Moody's credit rating agency last week downgraded its short-term rating, and on top of this a no-confidence vote is looming for the government within the next two weeks.
"At this point the key thing is to determine the bottom of the market," Hancocks said.

Meanwhile the PHILIPPINES' Finance Minister Roberto Ocampo starts an international roadshow in London on Monday to explain plans for rescheduling almost $2 billion of its Brady debt for uncollateralised Eurobonds. Mexico successfully pioneered such a move last April.
And VENEZUELA begins a European roadshow for a seven-year mark Eurobond in Dusseldorf.

Elsewhere in Europe, long-awaited elections take place in BOSNIA on Saturday. If the outcome is seen as acceptable to the West, it should help YUGOSLAVIA's attempts to return to the international fold from which it has been excluded due to its backing of Bosnia's Serbs.
Belgrade has been in discussion with the IMF and at the end of this week should have further talks with commercial creditors over rescheduling some $2 billion in debt.
The IFC emerging market composite investable index, IFC/IPRD, denominated in dollars, was off 0.3 percent, at 291.79 points, on Friday compared with a week ago.
Latin America was off 0.3 percent week on week at 291.79, Asia was down 0.9 percent at 248.03, while Europe, the Middle East and Africa rose 0.9 percent to 138.09.
